A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Language-Codec, and their text, equations, figures and tables support comparison. Material from v1 Appendices A–D is incorporated into corresponding main-text sections in v3; no material reading gaps prevent assessment.

before.justification: v1 reports original codec reconstruction experiments on LibriTTS and LJSpeech, plus objective and subjective evaluations of downstream zero-shot TTS, including appendix results.

after.justification: v3 reports original reconstruction and downstream TTS results, including additional controlled MCRVQ ablations with objective and subjective outcomes.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 adds multi-scale and complex STFT discriminators to the existing MPD/MRD setup, extending adversarial training. The encoder, Vocos-based decoder and masked quantization framework remain. Expanded descriptions of parallel quantization and fusion do not independently establish a new quantization procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 50,000-hour training mixture and evaluate LibriTTS Test-Clean/Test-Other reconstruction, LJSpeech generalization and LibriSpeech Test-Clean zero-shot TTS. Moving the comprehensive LJSpeech table from the appendix does not add dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated external baselines remain Opus, EVS, Lyra-v2, Encodec, Vocos and SpeechTokenizer, with the same codec comparisons within VALL-E and MobileSpeech. New Tables 4–5 introduce the explicitly evaluated Language-Codec w/o MCRVQ comparator, which substitutes Encodec-style RVQ.

E3.justification: The added ablation holds codec training steps and other configurations fixed while replacing MCRVQ with RVQ and retraining both downstream models. It also introduces subjective CMOS evaluation. Existing dataset splits, sampling rates, training budgets, prompting procedures and MOS sample/listener counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v1 evaluates the Vocos decoder and infers MCRVQ benefits indirectly from comparisons between complete systems. v3 retains that analysis and adds a direct, controlled MCRVQ removal experiment on both VALL-E and MobileSpeech, reporting WER, speaker similarity and CMOS in Tables 4–5. This substantially strengthens analysis of the central proposed component.

E5.justification: Both retain MOS reporting with ± values and the same stated sampling practice, without defining those uncertainties or reporting training seeds, repeated-run counts or statistical tests. Changes to MOS uncertainty values are result changes. The new CMOS table supplies point estimates without a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Language-Codec results change throughout the retained benchmarks. For example, eight-channel Test-Clean PESQ changes from 2.8546 to 3.6768, while four-channel Test-Other UTMOS decreases from 3.1096 to 3.0202. Downstream VALL-E/MobileSpeech speaker similarity changes from 0.6347/0.7283 to 0.6806/0.7544. These are revised-model results, not isolated same-model gains. v1 also has conflicting LJSpeech UTMOS values: Table 3 gives 3.7091/3.8955, whereas appendix Table 4 gives 3.8549/4.0127; v3 Table 2 reports 3.9461/4.2221. New ablation outcomes are added, while external baseline scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.3 adds explicit masking equations and revises the quantization factorization. Unlike v1 Equation 5, v3 Equations 6–7 explicitly subtract the sum of the first Nq quantizer outputs at the parallel-to-serial transition. This is a localized correction and extension of the formal description; no theorem or proof framework is added.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements add refined discriminator design and optimized hyperparameter selection to the claimed sources of improvement. The central claims about speech-language-model-oriented codecs, four-channel reconstruction, generalization and downstream TTS benefits retain their scope.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations involving discriminator gradient signals and attributes overall performance to data quantity/quality, hyperparameters and joint adversarial optimization. It interprets the new ablation as evidence that MCRVQ eases downstream codec generation. Conversely, v1's explicit limitation to speech-only training and validation is removed, although the discussion of prediction difficulties beyond four channels remains.

D1.justification: The reported code/model repository changes from speechnovateur/languagecodec_tmp to jishengpeng/languagecodec, and v3 additionally claims availability of a demo and best hyperparameter configurations. It specifies channel-wise fusion of embeddings/codebook vectors and adds instructions for dimension-specific MOS ratings. ConvNeXt and downstream training details already present in v1 appendices are retained through relocation.

R1.justification: v3 adds Mega-TTS and Boosting Prompting Mechanisms for Zero-Shot Speech Synthesis, with a short discussion of mel-spectrogram-based, decoupled modeling. Most expanded zero-shot TTS discussion comes from v1 Appendix A. The additional publication entry for Improved RVQGAN represents the same work already cited in v1.

P1.justification: v3 integrates all four appendices into related work, decoder description, experimental settings and generalization reporting. It substantially expands Section 3.3, reorganizes the ablation discussion and replaces the separate conclusion/limitations structure. Terminology changes from Mask to Masked Channel, and named authors replace the anonymous submission header.

P2.justification: The document is comprehensively reformatted from ACL to ACM style, changing typography, margins, running headers and caption presentation. The abbreviated LJSpeech table is removed and the full appendix table becomes main-text Table 2; two new ablation tables are added. Figure 1 retains the same architecture drawing.

improvement.justification: The controlled MCRVQ ablation provides more direct support for the central component than v1's indirect Vocos comparison, and the revised residual expression and integrated technical explanations improve clarity. Consolidated LJSpeech reporting also removes conflicting duplicate tables. These gains are tempered by removal of the explicit speech-only limitation and a new numerical error in Section 4.2: Table 1 implies PESQ/STOI margins of 0.5067/0.0255 over eight-channel SpeechTokenizer, whereas the prose states 0.03/0.5. The overall improvement is therefore useful but qualified.
